render.title: ATP yield from one glucose in aerobic respiration
render.body:
Complete aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule can yield approximately 30 to 32 ATP under typical cellular conditions. The exact number depends on the efficiency of the mitochondria and the shuttles used to move cytoplasmic NADH into the matrix.

Here is where the ATP comes from:

1. Glycolysis (cytoplasm): net 2 ATP directly, plus 2 NADH.
2. Pyruvate oxidation (mitochondrial matrix): 2 NADH (one per pyruvate, so two per glucose).
3. Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix, two turns per glucose): 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, and 2 GTP (equivalent to 2 ATP).
4. Oxidative phosphorylation (inner mitochondrial membrane): NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the electron transport chain. Each NADH yields roughly 2.5 ATP and each FADH2 roughly 1.5 ATP as protons flow back through ATP synthase.

Adding it up: 10 NADH x 2.5 = 25 ATP, plus 2 FADH2 x 1.5 = 3 ATP, plus 4 ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation (glycolysis and Krebs), gives a total near 32 ATP. The older textbook figure of 36 to 38 ATP assumed higher efficiency than cells actually achieve.

The key point is that oxidative phosphorylation — the electron transport chain combined with ATP synthase — accounts for the vast majority of the ATP made from one glucose molecule.
render.summary: Complete oxidation of one glucose can yield approximately 30-32 ATP under cellular conditions via glycolysis, Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.
